Robotic Process Automation in Business Process Management: A Systematic Literature Review and an Integrated Framework

# Robotic Process Automation in Business Process Management: A Systematic Literature Review and an Integrated Framework 

 by

## Abstract

Robotic Process Automation (RPA) has emerged as a significant technology within Business Process Management (BPM), yet the academic literature remains fragmented. This paper presents a systematic literature review (SLR) of RPA in BPM, conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines and synthesizing 83 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2015 and 2025. Systematic content analysis identifies six thematic dimensions: (1) process identification and selection; (2) implementation and life cycle management; (3) benefits and performance outcomes; (4) challenges and barriers; (5) technology integration; and (6) governance and organizational impact. These dimensions are synthesized into a conceptual integrated framework comprising three pillars—strategic alignment, operational execution, and continuous improvement—grounded in BPM theory and dynamic capabilities. The framework, while not empirically validated in this study, provides a theoretical foundation for future research and practice. Emerging themes include expanding sectoral breadth, empirical adoption model validation, and heightened focus on governance and sociotechnical work transformation. This review contributes a comprehensive thematic synthesis of RPA within BPM and offers a theory-grounded conceptual framework to guide researchers and practitioners in navigating intelligent process automation.

## 1. Introduction

Business Process Management (BPM) provides methods, frameworks, and technologies for designing, executing, monitoring, and improving organizational processes [1]. Organizations face mounting pressure to reduce costs, accelerate processing, and improve service quality under digital disruption. They must increasingly adopt technologies enabling rapid, scalable, cost-effective process change [2, 3]. Robotic Process Automation (RPA) has emerged as one of the most practically significant technologies in contemporary BPM.

RPA employs software robots (“bots”) to mimic human interactions with digital systems through the user interface (UI), automating repetitive, rule-based tasks without modifying underlying IT infrastructure [4, 5]. Unlike enterprise resource planning (ERP) implementations requiring months of configuration, RPA bots can be developed and deployed within weeks [6, 7]. The global RPA market is projected to exceed USD 13 billion by 2030 [8]. Early adopters in banking, healthcare, insurance, and public administration have reported substantial reductions in cycle times, error rates, and costs [5, 9].

However, organizations encounter difficulties in selecting automation candidates, governing bot portfolios, managing change, and aligning investments with strategic objectives [10, 11, 12]. Fragmented deployments yield local efficiencies but fail to generate enterprise-wide value when disconnected from coherent BPM thinking [4, 13]. Realizing RPA’s potential requires understanding it within a BPM context, not as a standalone IT initiative.

Several reviews have examined aspects of RPA and automation, yet none provides the BPM-theoretic integrative synthesis required to advance the field. The authors of Hofmann et al. [6] provide an early overview of RPA definitions and applications but do not adopt a BPM-centric lens or systematic methodology. The authors of Syed et al. [14] identify research themes and challenges in RPA but focus on technology-level concerns rather than BPM integration. The authors of Enriquez et al. [15] conduct a mapping study covering both scientific and industrial perspectives but do not develop an integrative theoretical framework grounded in BPM scholarship. The authors of Martínez-Rojas et al. [16] systematically map RPA and process mining integration but limit scope to this specific technology pairing.

This review differs from prior work in five critical respects. First, it adopts exclusive focus on the RPA–BPM intersection, positioning RPA explicitly within BPM theory rather than treating it as a standalone technology. Second, it employs rigorous systematic literature review methodology following PRISMA 2020 guidelines with explicit inclusion criteria, dual-screening protocol, and inter-rater reliability assessment ($
 
 κ
 =
 0.82
 
$). Third, it synthesizes recent literature (2015–2025) capturing the field’s rapid maturation beyond early exploratory studies. Fourth, it develops a theory-grounded integrative framework spanning strategic alignment, operational execution, and continuous improvement dimensions—not merely descriptive taxonomy. Fifth, it articulates an explicit research agenda addressing gaps in adoption theory, maturity models, and governance effectiveness. This positioning responds to calls for theoretically informed synthesis of emerging digital technologies in BPM [1, 2].

Despite industrial prominence and growing complexity, the academic literature on RPA within BPM lacks a shared conceptual foundation. Existing studies address isolated aspects—process selection [17, 18], life cycle management [19, 20], application domains [21, 22, 23], or governance [10, 11]—without offering an integrative perspective situating RPA within established BPM theory. Calls for theoretically grounded synthesis have grown [4, 6], yet no comprehensive systematic review applying rigorous methodology and BPM-theoretic lens has been conducted.

This paper addresses this gap through a systematic literature review conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines [24] and the concept-centric approach of Webster and Watson [25]. Analyzing 83 peer-reviewed articles, we identify six thematic dimensions and synthesize these into a conceptual integrated framework. Four research questions guide the review:

RQ1:
: How has RPA been studied and applied within BPM in the peer-reviewed academic literature?
RQ2:
: What thematic dimensions characterize the RPA–BPM intersection?
RQ3:
: What integrated framework can be used to organize these dimensions to guide research and practice?
RQ4:
: What are the implications of this synthesis for BPM research and practice?

This paper makes three contributions. First, it provides a comprehensive thematic synthesis of RPA within BPM, organizing fragmented knowledge into six coherent dimensions. Second, it develops a conceptual integrated RPA–BPM framework grounded in BPM theory and dynamic capabilities, offering a foundation for future empirical validation. Third, it identifies a structured research agenda advancing understanding of RPA as a BPM capability. This review responds to calls in BPM scholarship to develop theory-informed knowledge on emerging digital technologies in organizational process work [1, 2].

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides theoretical background. Section 3 describes methodology and findings. Section 4 introduces the conceptual framework. Section 5 develops implications. Section 6 concludes the study.

### 2.1. Business Process Management

BPM is broadly defined as an ambidextrous management discipline providing methods, technologies, and frameworks for designing, executing, monitoring, and continuously improving organizational processes to generate business value [1]. The authors of Zairi [26] organize BPM’s core concerns across three groups: business and process performance; consistent outcomes aligned with organizational objectives; and the use of resources, tools, and techniques for process management and control.

The authors of Rosemann and vom Brocke [27] identify six core BPM elements: strategic alignment, governance, methods, IT, people, and culture—elements that recur across all dimensions identified in this review. BPM success is moderated by contextual factors [2] and increasingly requires organizational agility in the face of digital disruption [3]. Recent scholarship positions advanced automation technologies—including process mining, AI, and RPA—as enablers of “intelligent BPM,” in which automation and analytics become integral to the BPM life cycle [1].

The resource-based view [28] and dynamic capabilities theory [29] offer complementary theoretical lenses for understanding RPA in BPM. From a resource-based perspective, RPA can constitute a process-level resource generating operational efficiency advantages. Resources generate sustained advantage when they are valuable, rare, inimitable, and non-substitutable (VRIN). From a dynamic capabilities perspective, the ability to identify, deploy, and continuously improve RPA initiatives constitutes a sensing and reconfiguring capability [29] that organizations can develop for sustained competitive advantage. This framing positions RPA not merely as a tool but as a capability-building mechanism within the broader BPM repertoire.

### 2.2. Robotic Process Automation

The IEEE Standards Association defines RPA as “a preconfigured software instance that uses business rules and predefined activity choreography to complete the autonomous execution of a combination of processes, activities, transactions, and tasks in one or more unrelated software systems” [30]. Bots operate by mimicking human interactions at the UI layer—navigating applications, extracting and entering data, executing rule-based decision logic—without requiring changes to underlying IT systems [4, 6]. This non-intrusive architecture renders RPA well-suited for “swivel chair” processes requiring data transfer across disparate systems, and for high-volume, structured, rule-dense workflows such as invoice processing, data reconciliation, and regulatory reporting [7, 13].

The RPA technology landscape is dominated by three major platforms—UiPath, Automation Anywhere, and Blue Prism—that have progressively integrated AI capabilities including natural language processing (NLP), computer vision, and machine learning (ML), extending automation to semi-structured and unstructured data [6]. This evolution has given rise to Intelligent Process Automation (IPA), which combines RPA’s UI-level execution with cognitive AI capabilities for more complex process scenarios [31]. The progressive integration of automation into enterprise resource planning (ERP) and accounting systems illustrates how RPA increasingly functions as an embedded component of digital infrastructure rather than a standalone tool [32].

Conceptually, RPA and BPM are complementary rather than substitutive. BPM operates from a holistic, top-down process design and re-engineering perspective, while RPA adopts a bottom-up, lightweight automation stance, automating processes as currently executed [4]. RPA does not replace BPM-driven process improvement; rather, it operationalizes BPM objectives at the task level, typically following process analysis and standardization [5, 33]. Frameworks for implementing RPA projects have been developed to address this life cycle complexity [34], and investment appraisal methods have been proposed to support the business-case development that precedes deployment [35]. This complementarity forms the conceptual anchor of our integrated framework.
